APP: pulse-relay
CURRENT PHASE: implementation_readiness_gate
PHASE PURPOSE: Before any code is written, audit whether the product brief, design handoff, iOS architecture, tech specs, project plan, and task contracts are coherent enough for a one-shot production build. Resolve blockers or explicitly downgrade scope before build starts.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

## Final Output

This phase confirms: **single-app build, no portfolio split.** The prompt asked for one native iOS app, and the concept that emerged from prompt_contract and product_research — a trust-graph-restricted, real-time pickup-relay coordination app for a school pickup pod — is inherently one app, not a decomposable set of sibling apps.

Selected app:
- **slug:** `pulse-relay`
- **category:** real-time trust-graph coordination / social-utility (explicitly not marketplace, not generic messaging, not "matching")
- **promise:** When a parent can't make pickup, their pod knows within seconds and exactly one person locks it in — no double coverage, no guessing who saw the message.
- **target user:** A parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster) hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict.
- **build:** true

Rejected alternatives: splitting into sibling apps (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app, a group-chat clone, a caregiver marketplace, a generic emergency-alert app); generic todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper reskins; single-user-only designs; open stranger/proximity matching; daycare/activity pod variants in v1; location-tracking-first designs. `portfolio_json` is null — this is not a portfolio parent.

Build-priority guidance carried into later phases: if build time is constrained, cut breadth in secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings polish) before ever compromising the correctness or speed of the two locked core funnels (post relay request → pod visibility; accept → conflict-resolve → complete), since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition.

{"phase": "initial_discussion", "one_paragraph_summary": "The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record. Two failure-mode requirements were elevated to core-loop, non-secondary status: acceptance is reversible until handoff completion, with an explicit release action that reopens the request and re-notifies the pod (~30s target), because an unretractable 'confirmed' state manufactures dangerous false certainty; and an unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (not silence or a static pending label), because silent ambiguity on an actually-open request is an equally dangerous failure mode. The data model was required to support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod (not a single-active-request assumption), even if the UI leads with a focused single card.   constraints: Any further palette changes must be surgical edits to Codex's existing token file, not a wholesale replacement
- [DEC-design_handoff-002] The request/card state machine distinguishes awaitingConfirmation (this device's own action in flight) from reconciling (state learned via a push-triggered refetch) as separate internal states sharing the pulse visual, plus queuedOffline (action taken with no connection, not yet in flight) and a distinct 'no longer open' state for a deep-link that resolves to a withdrawn/expired request — all four folded into the formal per-screen spec, not left as an inferred edge case.
  rationale: Collapsing awaitingConfirmation and reconciling into one case would make the losing device in the accept-race snap straight to 'already covered' with no pulse, destroying the exact side-by-side visual proof the two-phone demo depends on; queuedOffline and the expired-deep-link state prevent false or scary-looking states for two situations (offline compose, stale notification taps) that will happen routinely in real use.
  rejected: Treating reconciling as the same internal case as awaitingConfirmation; Rendering a queued offline action as a generic awaiting-confirmation spinner; Rendering an expired/withdrawn deep-link target as a generic error state
  constraints: Build must implement all four as named, distinct internal states, not just visually similar variants of two states
- [DEC-design_handoff-003] Screen graph and navigation are locked: AppGate resolves to AuthGate, PodOnboarding, or RelayBoard (default root); RelayBoard presents RequestComposer and RequestDetail as sheets, with RequestDetail also serving as the push deep-link destination; Profile and PodSettings are reachable only via stack push from the board header. No tabs, no additional navigation branches.
  rationale: Matches the narrow-screen-scope discipline already locked in design_discussion and keeps the IA aligned with the app's actual single-core-loop workload rather than adding chrome for an app with essentially one screen that matters.
  rejected: A tab-based root; Additional top-level navigation branches beyond the core loop and two secondary screens
  constraints: No later phase may add tabs or additional root-level navigation destinations
- [DEC-design_handoff-004] Motion timing is locked: the open-to-awaiting pulse is a 0.9s ease-in-out repeating breathing animation (scale 0.99→1.02 plus border alpha oscillation); resolution to either winner or loser uses an identical 0.45s mechanical spring latch (response 0.45, damping 0.82); Reduce Motion collapses both to a ~0.15s crossfade that preserves the text/icon state change; haptics never differentiate winner from loser as success versus warning/error.
  rationale: Codifies design_discussion's requirement that the accept-race loser reads as 'worked as designed' rather than a malfunction, down to exact animation and haptic values a build agent can implement without inventing anything.
  rejected: Distinct or error-styled haptic/motion treatment for the losing transition
  constraints: No implementation may give the loser transition a different duration, curve, or haptic category than the winner
- [DEC-design_handoff-005] If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft effort is spent in this order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — before any polish on the board resting state or secondary screens.
  rationale: Directly carries forward the craft-budget tiebreak already locked in design_discussion into this phase's concrete spec, so a build agent under deadline pressure has an explicit order rather than having to infer one.
  rejected: Leaving craft-budget priority unstated in this phase's own spec and relying solely on the prior phase's mention of it
  constraints: No craft time goes to secondary-screen or resting-state polish before all three named priorities are fully realized
- [DEC-design_handoff-007] The Relay HUD surface/neutral system is corrected to a warm-neutral palette (warm off-white backgrounds, warm charcoal dark surfaces) replacing the cool-blue scaffold from the earlier draft, while all state accent colors (amber pulse, teal confirmed, slate terminal, error red) remain unchanged.
  rationale: The neutral scaffolding, not the state accents, was the remaining source of the 'cold blue-black sci-fi HUD' register explicitly rejected in design_discussion's DEC-design_discussion-001; a cold base can trigger an alarm register even when state accents are correct.
  rejected: Keeping the blue-leaning neutral tokens on the grounds that state accents were already correct; Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm hex values, treated as confirming the same fix rather than a competing spec since both point the same direction
  constraints: All base surface/divider/background/card tones in Theme.swift must use the warm-neutral values in the final palette table; No non-tokenized neutral literals anywhere outside Theme.swift
- [DEC-design_handoff-008] Relay board request ordering is exclusively server-authoritative displayOrder (created-at ascending plus a deterministic backend tie-break); no client-side urgency computation or local re-sort exists anywhere in the spec.
  rationale: No urgency/severity/priority field exists anywhere in the locked data model; leaving 'urgency' in the spec language would hand a build agent an undefined sort key it would have to invent or silently drop, violating the playbook rule that no adjective may stand in for a number.
  rejected: Retaining 'sorted by urgency then age' as descriptive shorthand for age-driven sorting; Allowing client-side re-sorting as a fallback
  constraints: Board component renders request IDs in exact backend response order; Any future urgency concept requires an explicit new data-model decision in a later phase, not implicit inclusion here
- [DEC-design_handoff-009] Push notification payloads are never rendered as authoritative request state; every push is treated strictly as a wake-up signal that must trigger a targeted authoritative refetch of that specific request before any card transition occurs, and this is written as its own explicit architectural rule in the spec.
  rationale: Decoding and rendering directly from the notification payload is the fastest, most obvious implementation path for a competent iOS engineer, and it would pass every screenshot review and casual demo while silently breaking CAS correctness the first time APNs delivers pushes out of order or drops one — exactly the failure this app's core value proposition depends on not happening.
  rejected: Leaving the rule implicit in the existence of the 'reconciling' state without a standalone written line
  constraints: RequestDetail transitions to any terminal state must be gated on a real fetch result, never on notification userInfo contents; 'reconciling' remains an explicit, named state between wake-up and applied fetch result
  (supersedes DEC-design_handoff-006)
- [DEC-design_handoff-010] Connectivity and freshness edge cases are locked as explicit, named spec elements: queuedOffline is a state distinct from awaitingConfirmation; a single top-level (not per-card) 'Syncing latest pod state…' banner appears on launch/foreground and after a force-quit mid-action until the first fresh fetch of the session lands, with stale cache still rendering underneath for continuity; the elapsed-timer chip reads MM:SS under one hour then 'Xh Ym'; and the connection/session banner carries two distinct copy states (offline-with-queued-actions vs. uncertain-delivery) rather than one generic message.
  rationale: These are real, routinely-occurring situations (cold launch after force-quit mid-accept, spotty connectivity, sub-hour same-day timers) that directly affect user trust in what the screen is telling them, and leaving them implicit invites a build agent to render stale state with false confidence or collapse two meaningfully different situations into one vague message.
  rejected: Treating queuedOffline as a visual variant of awaitingConfirmation; A per-card syncing indicator instead of one top-level banner; An HH:MM:SS elapsed-timer format; A single generic 'connection issue' banner covering both offline-queued and uncertain-delivery cases
  constraints: Board-level syncing banner must appear whenever data freshness for the session is unverified; No terminal (latched/completed/withdrawn) card may be presented with full visual confidence before the first post-launch sync completes; No HH:MM:SS timer format anywhere in the app
- [DEC-design_handoff-011] No external Claude Design pass is used for this build; the design_handoff spec is implemented directly in SwiftUI, with the previously drafted upload prompt retained only as a future fallback for static, post-implementation assets (e.g. App Store imagery), never as part of the build's design-to-code path.
  rationale: The product's actual value lives in an interaction state machine (pulse/latch parity between the accept-race winner and loser), which a static mockup tool cannot represent or validate; a polished set of frames risks being mistaken for a validated interaction when it proves nothing about the one behavior this app is judged on.
  rejected: Commissioning an external Claude Design pass before build as an optional handoff-visual step
  constraints: Any future static-asset generation from the retained prompt must happen only after interaction implementation is complete and must not omit the reconciling/queuedOffline/deep-link-expired states
- [DEC-design_handoff-012] The canonical warm-neutral hex values are Codex's round-3 token set (background #F8F3EE/#121821, surface.card #FFFDF9/#1A2430, surface.strong #F2E9DD/#24303F, surface.divider #E7D9CA/#2E3F50, text.primary #2A221A/#EFF4FA, text.secondary #5B4E43/#9FA8B2, text.muted #7C7168/#87909A), adopted over Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm values since both target the identical fix and Codex's set was already the complete, fully-integrated token file.
  rationale: Two near-identical warm-neutral proposals arrived in the same round from parallel drafting; picking one concrete, already-fully-specified set avoids a further round over a few hex digits when both authors agree on the substantive direction.
  rejected: Running a fourth round solely to reconcile two very similar warm-neutral hex proposals
  constraints: Theme.swift must use exactly these hex pairs for the five neutral roles listed
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Adopt an actor-based RequestSyncCoordinator as the sole mutator of request state and push/queue reconciliation, with all in-flight transitions driven through a single deterministic reducer and an immutable enum state model (not booleans).
  rationale: Push wake-up and local user actions are concurrent by design; an actor plus enum-driven reducer makes illegal/racy state combinations structurally impossible rather than merely conventionally avoided, which is essential for the two-device accept-race proof to hold under real timing.
  rejected: Plain class/ObservableObject coordinator with shared-state mutation across multiple async paths; Boolean flag combinations for card states
  constraints: All request-card phase transitions must flow through the reducer/actor; no ad-hoc state flags anywhere in the client
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Session/auth material used by background refetch and force-quit-reconcile flows is stored in Keychain with accessibility kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly.
  rationale: Push wake-ups routinely arrive while the phone is locked; default whenUnlocked accessibility would silently block the authoritative refetch exactly when reconciliation matters most, directly undermining the 'flawless first incident' bar.
  rejected: Default whenUnlocked Keychain accessibility; Storing session tokens outside Keychain
  constraints: Background wake-triggered fetch path must be designed and tested against a locked-device scenario
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Remote notification authorization is requested only after successful sign-in and pod onboarding, with an explicit one-line rationale shown first; notification action buttons that trigger network actions directly are prohibited — deep-link-to-app is the only interaction surface from a push.
  rationale: Requesting permission before the user has context risks an unrecoverable denial; action buttons in Notification Center would let a build agent bypass the no-optimistic-confirmation contract since the notification center cannot render an awaiting-confirmation state.
  rejected: Requesting notification permission at cold launch; Notification action buttons (e.g. inline Accept) for accept/release/withdraw
  constraints: Every outcome shown to the user must come from a refetched, authoritative server state — never from notification payload or notification-center action results
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Critical Alerts entitlement remains fully unimplemented in v1 and is explicitly documented as feasibility-uncertain for a childcare-pickup-coordination app, not assumed to be obtainable in future roadmap language.
  rationale: Apple grants this entitlement selectively, historically to health/safety/security use cases with demonstrated need; treating it as a guaranteed future unlock would be a false dependency for the already-deferred DND-bypass subscription feature.
  rejected: Assuming the entitlement is obtainable and wiring related logic now; Adding entitlement-dependent branches into core v1 logic
  constraints: No v1 runtime code path may depend on Critical Alerts; any future pursuit must start with an Apple approval feasibility check
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] SwiftData board/request/receipt snapshots are treated as a disposable cache (purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch, no hand-rolled migration plan), while queued offline outbox actions must be durable enough to survive relaunch and app-version upgrades without silent loss — preserved separately or routed to an explicit recovery flow if a hard cache reset is required.
  rationale: Server is the sole source of truth for arbitration, so cache volatility is acceptable and cheap, but silently losing a user's queued intent (an accept/release/withdraw they already committed to) is a correctness failure, not an acceptable simplification.
  rejected: Building a full custom SwiftData migration plan for a cache that doesn't need persistence guarantees; Dropping queued outbox actions silently on cache invalidation
  constraints: On startup, stale cache renders for continuity only; terminal-state confidence requires a completed fresh fetch; Outbox durability must be verified across simulated app-version upgrade/relaunch scenarios
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] A backend-only concurrent integration test suite is required as an independent acceptance gate: two simultaneous HTTP accept calls against a real (test) CAS endpoint instance must deterministically yield exactly one success and one conflict response, plus a companion accept-vs-withdraw race test, both run with enough concurrency pressure to rule out a pass-by-luck result.
  rationale: A UI-driven two-simulator race test is subject to incidental timing jitter and can pass or fail by luck; only a dedicated backend-level concurrency test actually proves the database transaction/CAS logic is sound, independent of client wiring.
  rejected: Relying solely on the manual two-device demo as proof of CAS correctness; Treating a passing UI race test as sufficient mechanism verification
  constraints: This test must exist and pass before architecture/build signoff, in addition to (not instead of) the manual two-phone demo
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] No ML/AR/LLM stack and no third-party dependency expansion beyond Apple system frameworks (URLSession, SwiftData, AuthenticationServices, UserNotifications, OSLog) unless a specific, documented exception materially reduces CAS/push-path risk.
  rationale: The product's hard problem is state arbitration and reliability, not intelligent features; adding model-heavy or third-party tooling increases risk surface without addressing the actual failure modes this app must prove it avoids.
  rejected: Third-party networking/ORM libraries for developer convenience; Adding LLM/vision/AR hooks in v1
  constraints: Any future dependency proposal must include a one-line justification tied to CAS/push-path risk reduction, per the approved tech stack policy
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The primary push-driven reconciliation trigger is a visible alert push plus tap-driven deep link, or a foreground/background scenePhase-triggered refetch; silent content-available push is treated strictly as a best-effort bonus, never the backbone the app depends on for correctness.
  rationale: iOS can throttle or outright suppress silent background push under Low Power Mode or aggressive battery/thermal conditions, which is outside the app's control; leaning on it as the primary reconciliation path would make the 'flawless first incident' requirement depend on infrastructure behavior nobody can guarantee.
  rejected: Treating background content-available push as the primary reconciliation mechanism with visible push as a fallback
  constraints: Foreground/background scenePhase transitions must always trigger a board refetch regardless of whether a silent push was received
- [DEC-tech_specs-001] Canonical domain naming is the plain 'Request'-based family (Request, RequestStatus, RequestAction, ActionType, ActionResult, Receipt, Pod, PodMembership, User) rather than a Relay-prefixed family.
  rationale: Both participants independently landed here after swapping preferences mid-round-2; on reflection the plain family doesn't collide with anything in Foundation, avoids Hungarian-notation-style prefix repetition across every domain noun, and keeps types concise for both client and backend workers.
  rejected: Relay-prefixed family (RelayRequest, RelayAction, RelayReceipt, etc.); Keeping two parallel naming sets and reconciling per-type
  constraints: All build lanes must use exactly this naming; no lane may reintroduce a Relay-prefixed domain type
- [DEC-tech_specs-002] Expired-vs-withdrawn is represented by keeping RequestStatus at exactly 5 values (open, claimed, reopened, withdrawn, completed) and adding a separate closeReason: RequestCloseReason? field (autoExpired, requesterWithdrawn, systemHousekeeping), rather than adding a 6th status value.
  rationale: Cleanly separates 'what state is this row in' from 'why did it get here,' keeps the state-machine small, and leaves room for future system-driven reasons without ever touching the status enum again; the client's existing withdrawn card phase reads closeReason to pick copy so no 12th RequestCardPhase case is needed.
  rejected: Expanding RequestStatus to 6 values including a standalone 'expired' case; Silently dropping the expired/withdrawn distinction entirely
  constraints: RequestCardPhase must stay at exactly the 11 states locked in design_handoff; Auto-closure of a stale same-day request sets status=withdrawn plus closeReason=autoExpired, never a new status value
- [DEC-tech_specs-003] ActionType includes a required 6th case, reBroadcast, requester-only, allowed only from open/reopened status.
  rationale: DEC-initial_discussion-005 explicitly requires a re-broadcast path for an unfulfilled request; this had been dropped in one round-1 draft and needed to be explicitly restored and locked in both drafts.
  rejected: Treating re-broadcast as passive aging text with no user-triggered action; Overloading release or withdraw semantics to cover re-broadcast
  constraints: reBroadcast uses the same CAS-guarded action-write path as every other action type and updates lastRebroadcastAt
- [DEC-tech_specs-004] expectedRequestRevision is a required, non-optional UInt64 parameter on the action-write path (performAction and POST /requests/{id}/actions), threaded from OutboxAction through the coordinator to the wire endpoint; it stays optional only inside OutboxAction's storage model because that same model also queues brand-new post actions with no prior revision to guard.
  rationale: Prevents an offline device's queued action from replaying against an already-terminalized row with ambiguous results; making the parameter optional at the coordinator/API layer would let a future call site silently pass nil and defeat the entire guard.
  rejected: Optional expectedRequestRevision at the coordinator/API layer; Relying solely on the SQL WHERE clause without a corresponding required API parameter
  constraints: Every non-post action call must supply expectedRequestRevision; the coordinator must reject any call site that omits it for accept/release/withdraw/complete/reBroadcast
- [DEC-tech_specs-005] A third mandatory verification tier is added: a local coordinator-concurrency test where two independent RequestSyncCoordinator actor instances, each with a distinct fake identity, race an accept call via TaskGroup against one shared local test-backend instance, asserting the winner's event stream emits latchedConfirmed and the loser's emits latchedAlreadyCovered with the correct name populated.
  rationale: Neither the backend-only HTTP concurrency test nor the manual two-phone demo exercises the actual reducer and coordinator under real concurrent server responses; this tier is cheap to run in CI on every commit and is the only test that proves the reducer, coordinator, and real backend agree on the winner together, not each verified in isolation.
  rejected: Relying only on the backend HTTP concurrency test plus the manual two-phone demo
  constraints: This test tier must exist and pass before build signoff, in addition to (not instead of) the other two verification tiers already locked in ios_architecture_review
- [DEC-tech_specs-006] GET /api/v1/health is a required endpoint and must be the first call the client makes, gating any backend-dependent routing or state trust on canOperate/apiRevision/minClientVersion.
  rationale: Operationalizes the standing requirement (DEC-prompt_contract-008) that backend reachability be proven before any concept-specific schema or screen is trusted, as a concrete, testable contract-version handshake rather than an assumption.
  rejected: Assuming backend reachability without an explicit health/version-gate call; Deferring the reachability proof to ad hoc manual testing
  constraints: No backend-dependent screen or state may be trusted before this call succeeds
- [DEC-tech_specs-007] POST /api/v1/pods/join enforces a hard server-side single-pod-per-account cap in v1, returning 403 already_in_pod for a user with any existing PodMembership.
  rationale: Entitlement-gated multi-pod membership is explicitly out of implementation scope for this build (DEC-app_features-002); the only honest behavior is a hard server-side rejection rather than a silent allow that quietly builds an unrequested multi-pod feature.
  rejected: Silently allowing a second pod join with no server-side check; Leaving multi-pod-join behavior undefined and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: This cap must be enforced server-side, not just hidden client-side
- [DEC-tech_specs-008] Board ordering uses a single BIGSERIAL-backed displayOrder column as the sole sort key, exposed under that exact wire field name, with no compound tie-break and no client-side re-sort.
  rationale: A serial column can never produce a tie, so there's no tie-break logic to write, test, or get subtly wrong later; the wire field name matches what design_handoff already locked (DEC-design_handoff-008).
  rejected: A compound tie-break of createdAtUtc plus (serverRevision, id); A separate client-visible 'sequence' field distinct from the locked 'displayOrder' name
  constraints: Board component must render request IDs in exact backend response order; any future urgency concept requires a new explicit decision
- [DEC-tech_specs-009] RequestAction is a standalone, first-class audit-log table, written for every action attempt (post/accept/release/withdraw/complete/reBroadcast) regardless of applied-or-conflict outcome, and is never owned by or nested inside the Receipt object.
  rationale: Withdrawn and expired requests never produce a receipt by explicit prior design, so if the only place an action trail lived was nested inside a conditionally-absent receipt, every accept attempt on a request that ends in withdraw/expiry — including a losing accept that got a genuine conflict — would have no queryable record anywhere, violating the prompt_contract requirement that the audit/event log be a first-class object.
  rejected: Nesting an action trail array only inside the Receipt struct
  constraints: Receipt remains a derived read-time view, only constructible once a complete RequestAction row exists for that request
- [DEC-tech_specs-010] A queued/offline action that receives a conflict, forbidden, or unauthorized outcome from the server is terminal for that action — the coordinator moves it to an explicit error/resolved branch and stops retrying; only network/timeout failures are retriable.
  rationale: Blindly re-queuing a definitively rejected action (e.g. an offline accept replayed after the request was already claimed or withdrawn) would leave the UI in limbo and recreate exactly the false-confidence failure mode this app's entire state machine exists to prevent.
  rejected: Retrying all failed outbox actions uniformly regardless of failure type
  constraints: This distinction must be explicit in the reducer and covered by unit tests, not left as an implicit retry-loop detail
- [DEC-tech_specs-011] Two leftover infrastructure names are resolved by coordinator tie-break: the API client protocol is named RequestAPIClient (not PulseRelayAPIClient) and the shared error enum is named AppError (not RelayError); the module/file layout (App/Domain/State/Network/Persistence/Notifications/Features/Shared) is locked as proposed.
  rationale: Both names had drifted inconsistently in the final round despite both participants otherwise agreeing to drop Relay-prefixed naming; this is a cosmetic residual, not a substantive disagreement, so it's resolved directly rather than spending a fourth round on it, consistent with how the design_handoff phase resolved a near-identical near-duplicate hex-value proposal.
  rejected: Spending an additional round solely to reconcile two near-identical infrastructure names; Leaving both names inconsistent across build lanes
  constraints: All build lanes must use RequestAPIClient and AppError exactly as named
- [DEC-project_plan-001] Backend implementation stack is locked to Node.js + TypeScript with a thin HTTP layer and node-postgres (pg) against a managed Postgres instance, deployed to a real public HTTPS host already available in this workspace (Fly.io/Railway/Supabase/Neon-class); Milestone 0's exit criterion is an external curl of a real deployed /api/v1/health returning canOperate:true.
  rationale: Both participants independently converged on the same stack for the same reason: fastest path to a curl-provable, non-localhost health endpoint with minimal toolchain ceremony; Vapor was explicitly considered and rejected since domain types are hand-written on both sides regardless and it offers no compensating benefit in an unfamiliar toolchain.
  rejected: Vapor/Swift-on-server for stack symmetry with the iOS client; Leaving the backend stack/hosting choice unresolved and deferring it to ad hoc build-time decision
  constraints: No client screen or backend-dependent feature may be marked done before an external, non-localhost curl of /health succeeds; Exact hosting provider (Fly.io vs Railway vs Supabase-for-Postgres, etc.) is resolved at build time based on what's actually available in this workspace, not re-litigated in planning
- [DEC-project_plan-002] The physical two-device real-APNs demo remains the ideal acceptance artifact and must run exactly as locked in next_steps_small if a paid Apple Developer account, push-capable provisioning profile, and two physical devices are actually available in this build environment; if any of those is missing, the honest fallback is the backend HTTP concurrency test plus the local coordinator-concurrency test (both already hard gates) plus a two-simulator run using xcrun simctl push to inject the wake-up signal and visually observe the pulse-to-latch/already-covered-by-name transition, explicitly logged as 'push delivery simulated, not proof of real APNs infrastructure' and never presented as satisfying R-007/R-011.
  rationale: Real device push cannot be produced by the iOS Simulator under any circumstance, and requiring hardware/credentials that may not exist in this environment as an unconditional gate risks either blocking the project for reasons unrelated to app correctness or silently faking the result and misreporting it; the two already-locked concurrency test tiers independently prove the CAS/reducer correctness that the demo exists to showcase.
  rejected: Treating the two-device demo as an unconditional, non-negotiable gate regardless of environment; Silently substituting a simulator-injected push and reporting it as an unqualified pass of the real APNs demo-critical requirements
  constraints: Any simulator-based substitution must be explicitly labeled as simulated push delivery in verification output, never conflated with real APNs proof; The backend and coordinator concurrency test tiers remain mandatory regardless of which demo path is used
- [DEC-project_plan-003] Migration and seed work is a first-class, explicit sub-deliverable of the schema milestone (M2): numbered, idempotent SQL migration files applied in order by a trivial runner, plus an on-demand seed script/query that creates exactly two real user accounts already joined to one real pod.
  rationale: If seeding is a manual, ad hoc, multi-step process, the two-real-account verification protocol required by product_research and next_steps_small will get skipped under time pressure; a cheap, on-demand, re-runnable seed step is what keeps that protocol actually exercised throughout the build.
  rejected: Folding migrations/seeding into generic 'implement backend endpoints' work with no dedicated deliverable or exit criterion
  constraints: Migrations must be plain numbered .sql files, re-runnable from an empty database, no migration framework required; The seed script/step must be callable on demand, not a manual multi-step console process
- [DEC-project_plan-004] A dedicated, timeboxed verification/repair milestone (M8) runs after the demo gate (M7), specifically re-checking every core screen in both light and dark mode against Theme.swift for zero literal font/color/spacing values outside that file and zero placeholder/blank content, with fix time explicitly reserved rather than assumed to fall out of following the design spec.
  rationale: This fleet has two recorded incidents of exactly this failure pattern (hardcoded font size, hardcoded inline color) and five recorded blank/placeholder visual QA failures; 'the screens were built to spec' was insufficient evidence the last two times, so this phase must be its own gate with reserved repair time, not implied polish.
  rejected: Treating dark-mode/anti-literal/anti-placeholder checks as implicit outcomes of following the design spec during UI build; Folding this check into the demo milestone (M7) rather than giving it its own dedicated pass
  constraints: This milestone must have explicit time reserved for fixes found during the pass, not just for the check itself
- [DEC-project_plan-005] The full delivery plan is locked as nine sequenced milestones (M0 backend stack/hosting/health-gate, M1 contract freeze, M2 schema/migrations/seed/core writes, M3 CAS action endpoint, M4 iOS domain/coordinator core, M5 core UI build, M6 push/deep-link/offline hardening, M7 tiered verification demo, M8 dedicated verification/repair pass), each with a named exit gate, superseding the initial eight-milestone draft from round 1.
  rationale: Reconciles Codex's original eight-milestone skeleton with the three concrete gaps Claude identified (backend stack/hosting, tiered demo acceptance, explicit migration/seed and repair milestones) into one sequence both participants converged on.
  rejected: Treating milestone zero as 'backend architecture designed' rather than a proven, externally-reachable deployment; Leaving migration/seed and verification/repair as implicit sub-tasks of other milestones rather than named gates
  constraints: No milestone after M0 may be scheduled or trusted as complete until M0's external health-check exit criterion is met; M3 and M4's concurrency test tiers are hard gates independent of M7's device-demo outcome
- [DEC-task_assignments-001] Task granularity is locked to 33 fine-grained, file-scoped tasks (not milestone-level tasks), each mapped onto the owning_lane tags tech_specs already assigned to every type/endpoint.
  rationale: A task spanning dozens of files and a dozen requirement IDs (as in the original coarse draft) makes progress unobservable and effectively serializes a whole lane's work into one giant ticket; fine-grained tasks let four lanes run genuinely in parallel with checkable acceptance criteria.
  rejected: Coarse ~5-task milestone-level backlog
  constraints: Every future task added to this backlog should stay scoped to a handful of files with independently checkable acceptance criteria
- [DEC-task_assignments-002] Directory layout is locked as .agent_cwd/ios/PulseRelay/ (Xcode project/target named PulseRelay, App/ as the entry-point subfolder inside it) and .agent_cwd/backend/ (Node+TypeScript).
  rationale: An earlier draft used 'App' as both the Xcode project name and the entry-point subfolder name, which would collide in imports and Xcode's file picker; naming the project PulseRelay after the app's own slug removes the ambiguity.
  rejected: Naming the Xcode project/target 'App' with an App/ subfolder inside it
  constraints: All iOS file paths must be prefixed ios/PulseRelay/, never ios/App/
- [DEC-task_assignments-003] Branch and merge strategy is one branch and one PR per task, named feature/<lane>/<task-id>-<slug>, squash-merged into main once that task's own depends_on list and acceptance criteria are satisfied.
  rationale: With 33 fine-grained tasks, a single branch per lane would force logically independent tasks to fight over one branch's history; per-task branches keep each unit of work isolated and reviewable on its own.
  rejected: One long-lived branch per lane covering all of that lane's tasks

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.
